BREAKING: Global household net worth surged +7.3% YoY, to a record $570 trillion in 2025.

This was primarily driven by equities which accounted for 57% of the increase, while real estate contributed just 15%.

Since 2000, this figure has risen +338%, with an average annual increase of +5.9%.

As a result, global household net worth is now equivalent to ~380% of world GDP.

Real estate accounts for ~50% of the total, followed by equities and investment funds at ~25%, bonds and pensions at 20%, and cash deposits at 20%.

This is somewhat offset by loans, which equal ~15% of the full amount.

Among countries, US household net worth stood at $175 trillion last year, +133% above China's $75 trillion and +661% above Germany's $23 trillion.

Own assets or be left behind.

Foreign investors are piling back into South Korean equities:

Investors outside of South Korea purchased +$5.4 billion of South Korean stocks on Friday, the largest daily purchase on record.

Meanwhile, domestic retail investors sold a record -$5.5 billion of equities, marking their 3rd consecutive daily sale.

This marks a sharp reversal after foreign investors sold -$110 billion of Korean stocks in 2026 prior to Friday's session.

Over the same period, domestic retail investors purchased +$67 billion, including +$57 billion in May and June alone.

Furthermore, deposits held at Korean retail brokerages for stock purchases dropped -$23 billion from their June peak, to ~$74 billion.

Foreign capital appears to be returning to South Korea.

Foreigners now own a record 32.4% of Japan's stock market, the highest since Tokyo began tracking it in 1970.

The marginal owner of the Nikkei is foreign money, priced in the shakiest yen in decades. When the yen cracks, foreigners are the sellers, and they hold a third of the tape. $EWJ

The bond market is done waiting on the Fed to explain itself.

The 30-year Treasury just hit a 19-year high. The 2yr/30yr curve bear-steepened toward 100 basis points in weeks as traders dumped the long end. Options desks are now betting the 10-year tags 4.9% by August 21 and the 30-year clears 5.4%.

Warsh went dark, floated fewer Fed meetings, and offered no framework to fight inflation. So the market is repricing term premium on its own.

A 19-year high in the long bond is a higher discount rate on every stock, house, and corporate loan in America. When the bond vigilantes take the wheel, risk assets lose their floor.

$TLT

Wall Street is lending cash against stock that cannot be sold.

JPMorgan's private-bank loan demand jumped tenfold in months. Goldman's San Francisco loan balances are up 50% since 2023. Banks are writing share-pledge loans against pre-IPO AI paper, some as small as $150 million.

When banks chase paper this hard to win the next IPO mandate, you are late in the cycle.

The July jobs rebound is going to be a mirage.

Payrolls are expected to bounce to 85,000 after a weak 57,000 in June, with unemployment holding at 4.2%. Bloomberg Economics says the strength is borrowed: World Cup temp hiring is about to reverse, construction is soft, and fall hiring now leans on state and local governments with shrinking budgets.

A labor market this propped up by temporary jobs and tapped-out city halls is weaker than 4.2% makes it look. When those jobs roll off this fall, the real trend shows, and it points down.

Chile just showed you what stagflation does to a central bank.

Growth has printed negative for five straight months while inflation climbed back to 4.3% from 2.4% before the Iran war. The central bank is frozen at 4.5% for a fifth meeting, unable to cut into a shrinking economy because prices are rising.

This is the squeeze the oil shock sets everywhere: weaker growth and firmer inflation at the same time. A bank that cannot cut and cannot hike leaves the economy without relief and inflation without a brake, and Chile will not be the last one caught in it. $ECH

tweets.text: On this day in 1990, Iraqi tanks crossed into Kuwait before dawn, and Saddam Hussein seized one of the richest oil states on earth in a matter of hours. Oil markets ran the math instantly. Iraq and Kuwait together sat on close to a fifth of the world's proven crude, and now one man held it. A barrel that traded near $17 in July hit $46 by mid-October, a 171% jump in ten weeks. The US economy had already peaked that same month. The oil shock pushed it under, and the recession ran deep into 1991. Thirty-six years later the lesson holds. A fifth of the world's oil still moves through the Strait of Hormuz, and a single shock in that shipping lane can add dollars to every gallon and drop a soft economy straight into recession.
